name: Omar Haddad

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me both what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, could you tell me a bit about yourself?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Omar, I'm 27, and I manage the recruitment team for a big hotel group's regional office. There are six of us, and we hire housekeepers, chefs, porters and front desk staff for fourteen hotels. I live with my girlfriend Dana, who teaches Year 3 at a primary school, and we're slowly paying off my car loan. I also send my younger brother a bit each month toward his university rent.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Walk me through a normal working day. What do you actually do, what do you like, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mornings are the applications: sorting through a few hundred CVs, setting up interviews, chasing references. Afternoons I'm often out at one of the hotels, sitting with a head housekeeper who needs three people by Friday. I use AI now and then to write job adverts, because it's quicker than staring at a blank page. The best part is placing someone who's been out of work for a year. The worst part is the summer rush, when every hotel is short at once and they all blame us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's what I expected: handy for writing adverts, not much else. At work I'd say we should keep using it where it saves time and stop worrying. I'm not the type to post about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, my job would be fine, but my money still wouldn't be. Our pay here is lower than at the other hotel groups, and with the car loan and my brother's rent, there's not much left. We've got maybe two and a half weeks of savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going as I am, and keep using the AI for adverts and interview letters. I'd try to clear the car loan a year early by putting an extra fifty on it. And I'd ask Dana if we could start a small joint savings pot, even twenty a week.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Okay, mostly. A little stuck. AI isn't the problem in that picture, the bank balance is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which part of your work could AI take even in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The CV sorting, probably. We get maybe four hundred applications a week, and most are clearly wrong for the job. If a tool did the first sort, I'd lose one of my coordinators' main tasks, but I'd probably move them onto the hotel visits.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned your brother. How long will you keep sending him money?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two more years, until he graduates. My parents can't help much, so I said I would. My brother's university rent is about a hundred a month, which is exactly the amount I can't save.

say: AI is **handy for adverts**, not much else.
We should **keep using it** where it saves time and stop worrying.
think: My **job is fine**, but my money still isn't.
Car loan plus my **brother's rent** leaves about two and a half weeks saved.
do: Keep using AI for **adverts and letters**.
Put an **extra fifty** a month on the car loan.
Start a **joint savings pot** with Dana, even twenty a week.
feel: **Mostly okay**, a little stuck because of the bank balance.
S0.quote: My brother's university rent is about a hundred a month, which is exactly the amount I can't save.
fieldNote: His pressure is **family duty**, supporting his brother's studies.
He'd move a coordinator to **hotel visits** rather than cut them.
He sounds **pragmatic** and unbothered by AI itself here.

steps.text: Keep writing job adverts with the AI tool
Pay an extra fifty a month off the car loan
Keep sending his brother a hundred a month until graduation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second picture is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's a big change and we need to manage it sensibly. At work I'd argue that recruitment is about people, and the screening can go to software but the judgement shouldn't. I'd say it calmly, because I don't like drama.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my team gets cut in half. Writing, checking, booking and answering are all on the card, and that's most of what my coordinators do. I'd probably keep my job because I'm the one who knows the hotel managers, but it'd be a smaller job and maybe a smaller wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd do the company's training on the new recruitment software and become the person who knows it best. I'd start an HR qualification in employee relations, the part where you deal with disputes and grievances, because that's harder to hand to a computer. And I'd stop eating out completely until we had a month saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uncomfortable. I wouldn't be in a panic, but I'd feel like the ground is moving under me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who on your team would you worry about?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Jade, who's 24 and our youngest coordinator, spends most of her day booking interviews. Booking interviews is exactly the work that goes first, so I'd move Jade, our youngest coordinator, onto meeting new starters on their first day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you pay for the HR qualification?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The company sometimes pays half if your manager signs it off. I'd ask for that, and pay the rest monthly. If they said no, I'd wait a year rather than borrow.

say: This is a big change and needs **managing sensibly**.
Screening can go to software, but **hiring judgement** shouldn't.
think: My team probably **gets cut in half**.
I'd keep a **smaller job**, maybe with a smaller wage.
Knowing the **hotel managers** is what keeps me in the room.
do: Learn the **new recruitment software** better than anyone.
Start an **employee relations** qualification, half paid by the company.
Stop **eating out** until there's a month saved.
feel: **Uncomfortable**, like the ground is moving under me.
S1.quote: Booking interviews is exactly the work that goes first, so I'd move Jade, our youngest coordinator, onto meeting new starters on their first day.
fieldNote: He picks **employee relations** as the human part of HR to move toward.
He'd **wait rather than borrow**, which fits his steady nature.
He protects a junior colleague by **moving her role**, not fighting the change.

steps.text: Become the team's expert on the new recruitment software
Start an employee relations qualification with half the fees paid
Stop eating out until a month of savings is built

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third picture is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going too fast for people to cope, and the government needs to step in. At work I'd say we have to look after the hotel staff, because they're the ones with the least money. I'd vote on it, definitely.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I think head office recruitment is gone within a year of AGI. The hotels themselves would still need housekeepers and porters until the robots come around 2031, but the hiring could be done by software. My best bet would be getting out of the office and into a hotel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd apply for an assistant manager job at one of our hotels right away, because hotel operations is half hands-on and people-facing. I'd ask my brother to take a part-time job so I can stop sending money. And I'd cut everything except rent, food and the car loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Scared, in a quiet way. I'd keep it together for Dana, but I'd be awake at night doing sums.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would it be like asking your brother to support himself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Horrible, honestly, he's in his last year and working is hard with exams. But two years' warning doesn't leave me a choice. I'd tell him straight, the way our dad told us things.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Dana's teaching job feel safer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Safer than mine, yes, for now. Kids still need a person in the room, so my girlfriend Dana's teaching job feels safer than mine. But a lot of her marking and planning is thinking work too, so she might end up with more children per class.

say: It's **too fast** and the government needs to step in.
We must look after **hotel staff**, who have the least money.
think: **Head office recruitment** is gone within a year of AGI.
Hotels still need **hands-on staff** until robots, around 2031.
do: Apply for an **assistant hotel manager** job right away.
Ask my brother to take a **part-time job**.
Cut spending to **rent, food** and the car loan.
feel: **Quietly scared**, holding it together for Dana but awake doing sums.
S2.quote: Kids still need a person in the room, so my girlfriend Dana's teaching job feels safer than mine.
fieldNote: He moves toward **hotel operations** because it's partly hands-on.
Asking his brother to work is the **hardest cut** he names.
He thinks Dana's job is safer but expects **bigger classes**.

steps.text: Apply for an assistant manager job at one of the group's hotels
Ask his brother to cover his own rent with a part-time job
Cut spending to rent, food and the car loan
Vote for whoever promises income support

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth picture is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years means companies can't claim they were surprised. I'd want our HR department to have a plan for every team by next year. I'd say it in meetings, politely but more than once.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd stay in recruitment for two or three years while it still pays, then move. By 2031 the office work is gone, so I need to be in a hotel by then. Hotels give me until about 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the employee relations qualification, then aim for a hotel operations role by 2029. My brother would have graduated by then, so that hundred a month goes into savings. I'd want three months saved before we think about a wedding.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Worried, but steadier. Five years is enough time to make one big move properly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why the wedding?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dana and I have talked about getting married in a couple of years. Weddings cost a fortune, and with my job wobbling I wouldn't want to spend our savings on one big day. We'd probably do something small.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would stop you moving into a hotel role?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that everyone from head office would have the same idea. If fifty people from head office apply for one hotel job, I need to be first. That's why I'd move a year earlier than I need to.

say: With five years' notice, companies **can't claim surprise**.
HR needs a **plan for every team** by next year.
think: Stay in recruitment **two or three years** while it pays.
A **hotel role** buys me until about 2034.
do: Move into **hotel operations** by 2029, ahead of the crowd.
Save the brother's **hundred a month** once he graduates.
feel: **Worried but steadier**, with time for one big move.
S3.quote: If fifty people from head office apply for one hotel job, I need to be first.
fieldNote: He plans to move **a year early** to beat the crowd.
A **smaller wedding** is his quiet trade-off.
He thinks clearly about the **three-year robot gap** in hotels.

steps.text: Finish the employee relations qualification by 2028
Move into a hotel operations role by 2029
Plan a small wedding instead of a big one
Save his brother's hundred a month after graduation

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last picture is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a fair amount of time, and people should use it calmly. At work I'd suggest we start retraining staff now, slowly, without scaring anyone. I'd probably not say much more than that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, ten years makes me feel like I can plan properly. I'd be 37 when AGI comes, maybe with a child. I'd want to be a hotel general manager by then, or in a role where you handle people face to face.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stay where I am for now and keep learning the new tools. I'd do the employee relations qualification over two years and apply for hotel jobs from about 2030. We'd get married in 2028 and save for a deposit after that.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fairly calm, with some worry in the background. Ten years is long enough that it feels like normal career planning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said fairly calm. What's the worry in the background?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Everyone treats ten years like forever, and then it's 2035 and we're all in the same mess. I don't trust the company to plan that far ahead.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you buy a house in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe around 2031, once I'm in a hotel role. I wouldn't buy while I'm in head office. Dana's job is steadier, so the mortgage would probably be based on her pay.

say: Ten years is **fair**, and people should use it calmly.
Start **retraining staff** now, slowly, without scaring anyone.
think: Ten years means I can **plan properly**.
By 37 I want to be a **hotel general manager**.
Face-to-face **people work** is where I'd feel safest.
do: Keep learning the **new tools** in my current role.
Get married in **2028**, then save for a deposit.
feel: **Fairly calm**, with background worry that nobody plans ahead.
S4.quote: Everyone treats ten years like forever, and then it's 2035 and we're all in the same mess.
fieldNote: He treats the decade as **normal career planning**.
His worry is **institutional delay**, not his own effort.
He'd base any **mortgage** on Dana's steadier pay.

steps.text: Keep learning the new recruitment tools in his current role
Apply for hotel management jobs from about 2030
Marry Dana in 2028 and then save for a deposit

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My job is all office work, I support my brother, and we've got almost nothing saved. What would help is the company giving office staff first chance at hotel jobs, and some help with retraining costs.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Maybe ask about people who send money to family. A lot of us at my level are quietly helping parents or siblings, and that's money we'd need if things went wrong.

headlineQuote: A lot of us at my level are quietly helping parents or siblings, and that's money we'd need if things went wrong.
portrait: Omar is 27 and runs a **six-person recruitment team** for a hotel group's regional office.
He lives with Dana, a **primary teacher**, and sends his brother money each month.
He uses AI now and then for **job adverts** and adapts once things are proven.
His escape route in every AGI picture is **hotel operations**, which is partly hands-on.
He stays **pragmatic**, moving from uneasy to alarmed as the timeline shortens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028**, because his office job goes and family support drains savings.
whatWouldHelp: First chance at **hotel jobs** for head office staff.
